analysis.title: US Midterm Elections: what to expect and what the market impact could be
key_insights: CACIB handicaps the 3 November 2026 midterms at 65% Democratic sweep, 25% Democratic House/Republican Senate, 10% Republican sweep. A Republican House/Democratic Senate split is called highly unlikely.

House: odds of about 90% that Democrats retake control. Republicans hold 220-215 (vacancies assigned to the prior holder), so Democrats need a net gain of at least 3 seats. The generic ballot favours Democrats by more than 8ppt, against a 2.6ppt Republican win in the 2024 House vote, a swing of close to 11ppt.
Redistricting has limited the seats truly in play to the 20s, so a wave of 40+ seat gains is highly unlikely even though the 3-seat bar is low.
Trump's approval is below 40%, more than 20ppt underwater. Net approval is -32.4ppt on the economy and -43.8ppt on inflation, and now -10.6ppt on immigration.

Senate: Republicans hold 53-47 and Democrats need a net gain of 4 seats, since a 50-50 tie is broken by VP Vance. CACIB puts Democratic Senate odds at about 65%. Toss-ups include Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas. North Carolina is rated Likely D and New Hampshire Lean D.

Legislative gridlock is expected if Democrats win the House, whatever the Senate result, because of the filibuster and the presidential veto. A Senate win would mainly matter for blocking judicial and other appointments and for oversight and investigations.

Impeachment is possible but treated as noise, since removal needs a two-thirds Senate majority. Tariffs and foreign policy are not expected to change much, because Trump relies on previously delegated authority and the veto. There is a decent chance of another government shutdown next year.

Rates: divided government would reduce the odds of major spending programmes and tax cuts. That eases pressure on term premium and long-end yields, which is supportive of lower long-end yields and a flatter curve. Front-end yields stay high because energy prices are elevated and the Fed is likely to deliver more hikes.

The FY2026 federal deficit was USD1.99trn (about 6% of GDP) on USD7.4trn of spending (up 6%) and USD5.4trn of revenue (up 3%), against USD1.775trn in FY2025 and USD1.817trn in FY2024. CBO projects debt-to-GDP rising from 100% to 120% within a decade.

FX history since 1976: a Democratic Congress with a GOP president has typically meant a weaker USD in the following months. A GOP president and Senate with a Democratic House has typically meant a USD rally, most recently after the 2018 midterms with a recovering economy and a hawkish Fed.

The CACIB main FX scenario is cyclical convergence between the US and the rest of G10, a USD smile/smirk. It cites slowing AI investment and a possible AI stock correction, gridlock and fading fiscal support, lower energy costs, repatriation flows into EUR and JPY, and Fed cuts in H2 2027. The risk scenario is an AI boom-bust, a persistent energy shock and a US or global recession or stagflation.

Emerging markets: the midterms are likely not a game changer. Three channels are fiscal and growth, Iran and oil, and the AI trade. Effects are ambiguous, since Trump could become more assertive on Iran to rally his base or have less room to spend on it.

EM backdrop: retail sales and industrial production are resilient, exports are accelerating on chips, AI and commodities, and the EM-DM carry gap is decent. China's 2026 GDP growth is expected at 4.6%, and the midterms are not a game changer there because of bipartisan consensus on capping China's rise.

macro_indicators.interpretation: The deficit is exceptionally large for a period without recession or crisis, which supports term premium pressure absent a fiscal brake from gridlock.
Spending growth is outpacing revenue growth.
Revenue is growing at half the rate of spending.
Even 6% real GDP growth with 5% interest rates would be needed just to stabilise debt.
The front end stays high because of the elevated energy prices and expected Fed hikes.
Long yields are expected to stay above 5% through most of 2027.
The long bond is seen near 5.4% for most of the forecast horizon.
Targeted stimulus and exports offset a difficult domestic growth equation.

risk_factors: AI boom-bust ending in a global market selloff.
A persistent negative energy shock hurting global growth.
A global or US slowdown, potentially a recession or stagflation.
Large deficits and rising debt could keep term premium elevated.
Political gridlock plus unchanged foreign policy poses downside risks to the US economic outlook and the USD.
charts_described: Generic congressional ballot chart: Democrats lead by more than 8ppt, a swing of close to 11ppt from the 2024 House vote.
Trump approval chart: approval below 40%, more than 20ppt underwater against disapproval.
Senate race table: North Carolina Likely D with Cooper +10.6 in the RCP average, New Hampshire Lean D with Pappas +6.5, and toss-ups in Alaska, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas.
EM-DM carry gap chart: EM implied yield 430bp versus US 3M SOFR 120bp, a spread of 311bp.
vol_and_positioning: Foreign investors have been buying US stocks but not US Treasuries, according to the capital flow chart.
Market betting odds ahead of the midterms price a Democratic sweep.
geopolitical: Iran: a Democratic Congress could constrain Trump's funding and leeway, which could ease oil prices, or he could become more assertive to boost his base, which could lift oil.
The Democratic Congress is seen as unlikely to change tariff policy, because Trump uses previously delegated authority and the veto.
Democratic Senate control could mean more oversight of the executive and frustrate Trump's foreign policy.
China: there is bipartisan consensus on capping China's geoeconomic ascent, so the midterms are not a game changer.

tension_points.bull_case: History shows the USD weakened after midterms that produced a Democratic Congress with a GOP president. Gridlock and fading fiscal support add to the case for USD weakness, in line with the CACIB cyclical convergence scenario.
tension_points.bear_case: With a GOP president and Senate and a Democratic House, the USD rallied across the board after the 2018 midterms, when the economy was recovering and the Fed was hawkish.
tension_points.what_invalidates: US growth outperformance with an AI boom and a hawkish Fed would revive the USD, as would a risk-aversion spike from an AI bust or recession.

tension_points.bull_case: Gridlock reduces the odds of major spending programmes and tax cuts, easing term premium and supporting lower long-end yields and a flatter curve.
tension_points.bear_case: The deficit of about 6% of GDP and debt heading to 120% of GDP keep term premium pressure on long yields, and the front end stays high on energy prices and Fed hikes.
